learn.hook: Your morning cup of chai needs a tea farmer in Assam, a truck driver, a shopkeeper and a price you can afford. Who studies how all these people and places are linked? Social scientists do!
points: Social science is the careful, systematic study of human society: how people live together, work, make rules, use resources and change over time.
In Classes 9 and 10 it is studied through four main disciplines: History, Geography, Political Science and Economics.
History studies the human past and how things changed; Geography studies places, location and how people and the environment affect each other.
Political Science studies governance, institutions, power and how public decisions are made; Economics studies how people make choices about limited resources.
Social science depends on evidence. A good social scientist separates personal opinion from claims that can be supported by facts.

example.q: Think it through: A new bus route starts in your town. Which question would each social science discipline ask about it?
steps: Geography: Which places and villages does the route connect, and why was this road chosen?
Economics: How much does a ticket cost, and who can now reach jobs or markets more cheaply?
Political Science: Who decided to start the route, and how did the local government make the decision?
History: How did people of this town travel twenty or fifty years ago, and what has changed?
example.answer: Each discipline looks at the same event from a different angle: place, money and choices, decision-making, and change over time.

learn.reallife: When you read a newspaper story about floods, elections, prices of onions or an old fort being restored, you are reading social science in action.

The four main social science disciplines in Classes 9 and 10 are History, Geography, Political Science and Economics.

quiz.q: Which of these best describes social science?
options: The study of chemicals and their reactions

The study of numbers and shapes

steps: Social science studies people in society
how they live, work, govern themselves and use resources
Chemicals, numbers and plants belong to the natural sciences and maths
Answer: The systematic study of human society and relationships

steps: Meera's question compares rainfall in two places

quiz.q: Which discipline studies how people make choices about limited resources such as money, time and land?
quiz.explain: Economics studies production, exchange, distribution and the choices people make because resources are limited.
steps: Resources like money, time and land are limited
Economics studies the choices people make because of this

quiz.q: A student studies how a panchayat plans a new village well and who takes the final decision. Which discipline is this?

How decisions are made by bodies like panchayats is part of Political Science

Answer: Political Science

quiz.q: Which is a statement based on evidence rather than opinion?
options: Old forts are boring to visit
Village life is better than city life
Cricket is the best sport in the world
The census counts the population of India
quiz.explain: That the census counts India's population can be checked. The other statements are personal preferences.
steps: Evidence can be checked; opinions are personal preferences
'Boring', 'better' and 'best' are opinions
That the census counts India's population can be checked
Answer: The census counts the population of India
quiz.mistake: Treats personal likes and dislikes as facts

quiz.q: Why do social scientists study the same event from several angles?
options: Because one angle usually gives an incomplete picture
Because they like making things complicated
Because each discipline gives the same answer
quiz.explain: A flood, for example, has geographical, economic, political and historical sides. Looking at all of them gives a fuller understanding.
steps: One angle usually shows only part of an event
A flood has geographical, economic, political and historical sides
Looking at all of them gives a fuller picture
Answer: Because one angle usually gives an incomplete picture
quiz.mistake: Assumes one discipline can explain every part of a social event

quiz.q: Which question would a historian most likely ask about a village market?
options: How much profit does each stall make today?
Which soil type is found around the market?
How has the market changed over the last hundred years?
Who votes in the panchayat election?
quiz.explain: Historians study change over time, so they ask how the market looked and worked in the past.
steps: Historians study change over time
So a historian asks how the market has changed over the last hundred years

Answer: How has the market changed over the last hundred years?

quiz.q: What does 'social interdependence' mean?
options: Every family grows all its own food and makes all its own things
People depend on one another to meet their everyday needs
quiz.explain: A simple meal needs farmers, transporters and sellers. People rely on each other's work.
steps: A simple meal needs farmers, transporters and sellers
People rely on one another's work
That is social interdependence
Answer: People depend on one another to meet their everyday needs

teach.nudge: But which subjects are part of social science, and how do social scientists know they are right?

topics.title: How we know about the past: sources and evidence

learn.hook: A coin found in a farmer's field in Andhra Pradesh can tell us which king ruled, what language was used and how far traders travelled. Clues like this are a historian's treasure.
points: Historians use sources: things from the past that give evidence about it.
Archaeological sources are material remains such as tools, pottery, beads, buildings, terracotta figurines and fossils, found by careful excavation.
Epigraphic sources are inscriptions carved or written on hard surfaces such as rock, pillars or copper plates; numismatic sources are coins.
Written (literary) sources include texts such as the Arthashastra, credited to Kautilya; oral traditions, songs and family records (genealogies) also preserve memory of the past.
Every source must be checked. Historians compare sources and ask who made them and why. Scientific methods such as carbon-14 dating help find the age of ancient remains.

example.q: Think it through: An old copper plate records a king giving land to a village temple. What can a historian learn from it, and what should she be careful about?
steps: It is an epigraphic source, because the record is engraved on metal.
It can show the king's name, the language and script used, place names and how land was granted.
It was written on the king's orders, so it may praise the king more than ordinary people would.
She should compare it with other sources such as coins, other inscriptions and excavated remains.
example.answer: It gives useful evidence about rulers, language and land grants, but it must be checked against other sources because it shows the ruler's point of view.

learn.reallife: Museums such as the National Museum in New Delhi display coins, seals, pottery and inscriptions, and each label tells you what kind of source it is.

quiz.q: A silver coin with a ruler's name is found at an old site. What type of source is it?
quiz.explain: Coins are numismatic sources. They can show rulers, metals used, symbols and trade links.
steps: The object is a coin with a ruler's name
Coins are numismatic sources
They show rulers, metals, symbols and trade links
Answer: A numismatic source
quiz.mistake: Mixes up coins (numismatics) with inscriptions (epigraphy)

quiz.q: Words carved on a rock or stone pillar are an example of which source?
quiz.explain: Inscriptions on hard surfaces like rock, pillars or metal plates are epigraphic sources.
steps: The words are carved on rock or a stone pillar
Inscriptions on hard surfaces are epigraphic sources
Coins would be numismatic
Answer: Epigraphic
quiz.mistake: Thinks any old object with writing is a coin or a book

quiz.q: Which of these is an archaeological source?
options: A folk tale told by a grandmother
A terracotta figurine dug up at a site
A family tree written in a register
A song sung at a festival
quiz.explain: Archaeological sources are material remains such as figurines, pottery, tools and buildings found through excavation.
steps: Archaeological sources are material remains found by digging
A terracotta figurine dug up at a site is such a remain
Folk tales and songs are oral sources
Answer: A terracotta figurine dug up at a site
quiz.mistake: Confuses material remains with oral or written sources

quiz.q: Which text on administration, taxation and the duties of rulers is credited to Kautilya?
quiz.explain: The Arthashastra, credited to Kautilya, discusses statecraft, administration and economic management.
steps: The text deals with statecraft, administration and taxation
It is the Arthashastra
credited to Kautilya
Answer: Arthashastra
quiz.mistake: Mixes up well-known ancient texts and their subjects

quiz.q: Why do historians compare several sources about the same event?
options: Because one source may be incomplete or show only one point of view
Because older sources are always wrong
Because only coins can be trusted
quiz.explain: A single source can be biased or incomplete. Comparing sources helps historians reach a more reliable picture.
steps: A single source may be biased or incomplete
Comparing several sources shows other points of view
This gives a more reliable picture
Answer: Because one source may be incomplete or show only one point of view
quiz.mistake: Believes any one source tells the full, unbiased truth

quiz.q: Which scientific method helps find the age of ancient remains such as bones, wood or charcoal?
quiz.explain: Carbon-14 dating measures how much radioactive carbon is left in once-living material to estimate its age.
steps: Bones, wood and charcoal were once living material
Carbon-14 dating measures the radioactive carbon left in them
That estimates their age
Answer: Carbon-14 dating
quiz.mistake: Does not know that science helps historians date the past

quiz.q: A record listing the births and marriages in a family over many generations is called a
quiz.explain: Genealogical records trace family lineage across generations.
steps: The record traces births and marriages across generations
A record of family lineage
is a genealogical record
Answer: genealogical record
quiz.mistake: Does not recognise family records as a historical source

quiz.q: A king's inscription says he was the greatest ruler on earth. What should a careful historian think?
options: It must be completely true because it is carved in stone
Inscriptions are useless and should be ignored
Only the king's enemies can be trusted
It is useful evidence but may exaggerate, so it should be checked
quiz.explain: Royal inscriptions were often written to praise the ruler. They are valuable, but their claims must be compared with other evidence.
steps: Royal inscriptions were often written to praise the ruler
So the claim may be exaggerated
It is useful evidence, but it should be checked against other sources
Answer: It is useful evidence but may exaggerate, so it should be checked
quiz.mistake: Accepts or rejects a source completely instead of weighing it

teach.ask: Gappu found an old coin under his nest. 'How can a tiny coin tell anyone about the past? And what other clues do historians use?'
teach.praise: Wow! Coins, inscriptions, remains and texts are all sources, and historians compare them to check the truth. I'll guard my coin carefully!
teach.nudge: Nice start! But should a historian believe one source straight away, or do something else first?

revise.summary: Historians learn about the past from sources: archaeological remains, inscriptions, coins, written texts and oral traditions. Every source must be checked and compared, because one source may be incomplete or show only one point of view.
focus: Classify a source as archaeological, epigraphic, numismatic, written (literary) or oral/genealogical
Explain why historians compare sources and ask who made them and why
Know that carbon-14 dating helps find the age of ancient remains
remember: Archaeological: material remains (tools, pottery, beads, buildings, terracotta figurines, fossils) found by excavation
Epigraphic: inscriptions on rock, pillars or copper plates; numismatic: coins
Arthashastra: a text on administration, taxation and duties of rulers, credited to Kautilya
Genealogy: a family record of births and marriages over many generations
traps: Don't mix up coins (numismatics) with inscriptions (epigraphy)
Don't believe any one source tells the full, unbiased truth
Don't accept or reject a source completely; weigh it and check it

topics.title: How history, geography, civics and economics connect

learn.hook: When the monsoon fails in a village in Marathwada, crops dry up, families lose income, the government plans relief and some people migrate. One drought, four subjects!
points: Real problems rarely fit into a single subject. Studying them using several disciplines together is called an interdisciplinary approach.
Geography gives the spatial perspective: where something happens and why that location matters, using maps, globes, atlases and GIS.
Economics shows effects on incomes, prices and jobs; Political Science shows how governments and local bodies such as panchayats respond.
History shows how a place or problem has changed over time, for example how settlements grew after farming and the taming of animals began.

Ideas from India's past, such as vasudhaiva kutumbakam ('the world is one family'), remind us that societies everywhere are connected. Sustainable development means meeting today's needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

example.q: Think it through: India has a long coastline. How can this one geographical fact connect to history and economics?
steps: Geography: a long coastline gives many natural harbours and access to the sea.
History: for thousands of years ships from Indian ports traded with distant lands, carrying goods and ideas.
Economics: ports create jobs in fishing, shipping and trade, and goods can be exchanged with other countries.
So a fact about location helps explain past events and present livelihoods.
example.answer: The coastline (geography) made sea trade possible in the past (history) and supports jobs and trade today (economics).

learn.reallife: Planning a new metro line in a city needs maps (geography), budgets (economics), government approval (political science) and knowledge of old buildings in the way (history).

geography, economics, political science and history

quiz.q: What does the 'spatial perspective' in geography focus on?
options: Where something is located and why that location matters
quiz.explain: Spatial means related to space or location. Geographers ask where things are and why.
steps: 'Spatial' means related to space or location
Geographers ask where something is
and why that location matters
Answer: Where something is located and why that location matters
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'spatial' with 'special' or with time

quiz.q: What does vasudhaiva kutumbakam mean?
quiz.explain: This ancient Sanskrit phrase expresses the idea that all people of the world are like one family.
steps: Vasudhaiva kutumbakam is an ancient Sanskrit phrase
It says all people of the world are like one family
So it means 'the world is one family'
Answer: The world is one family

quiz.q: Which tool would a geographer use to study land use with computer maps and layers of data?
quiz.explain: GIS combines maps with data, for example showing rainfall, roads and villages together.
steps: GIS combines computer maps with layers of data
such as rainfall, roads and villages
A geographer would use GIS for land use
Answer: GIS (Geographical Information System)
quiz.mistake: Does not link GIS with mapping

quiz.q: In a drought, which question belongs to Economics?
options: How did the farmers' incomes change?
What were droughts like a century ago?
quiz.explain: Income, prices and jobs are economic questions.
steps: Economics deals with income, prices and jobs
How farmers' incomes changed is such a question
River basins, ministries and past droughts belong to other disciplines
Answer: How did the farmers' incomes change?
quiz.mistake: Cannot tell economic questions from geographical or political ones

quiz.q: Which is the best meaning of sustainable development?
options: Using up all resources as fast as possible
Stopping all development to save nature
Meeting present needs without harming future generations' ability to meet theirs
Developing only cities and not villages
quiz.explain: Sustainable development balances today's needs with the needs of people in the future.
steps: Sustainable development balances two sets of needs
It meets present needs
without harming future generations' ability to meet theirs
Answer: Meeting present needs without harming future generations' ability to meet theirs
quiz.mistake: Thinks sustainability means either no development or unlimited use

quiz.q: Panchayati Raj is often used as an example of which idea in Political Science?
options: Democracy at the grassroots, with local people taking part in decisions
quiz.explain: Panchayati Raj lets villagers take part in local planning and decisions, which is democracy at the grassroots level.
steps: Panchayati Raj lets villagers take part in local planning and decisions
People sharing in decisions at the local level
is democracy at the grassroots
Answer: Democracy at the grassroots, with local people taking part in decisions
quiz.mistake: Does not connect local self-government with Political Science

quiz.q: Why does a historian studying the growth of a town also need geography?
options: Because geography is the same as history
Because rivers, land and climate influence where and how towns grow
quiz.explain: Physical features like rivers and fertile land help explain why towns grew in particular places.
steps: Towns grow where physical conditions suit them
Rivers, fertile land and climate influence where and how towns grow
So a historian of a town also needs geography
Answer: Because rivers, land and climate influence where and how towns grow
quiz.mistake: Studies change over time without considering the place where it happened

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: 'Why can't I learn history in one box and geography in another box? Why do people say they are connected?'
teach.praise: Tweet! A real problem like a drought has many sides, so we join the subjects together to see the full picture. Got it!
teach.nudge: Can you give me an example of one problem and show how two or more subjects help explain it?

revise.summary: Real problems rarely fit into one subject, so social scientists study them using several disciplines together: an interdisciplinary approach. Geography gives the 'where', History the change over time, Economics the effects on incomes and jobs, and Political Science how governments respond.
focus: Use the term interdisciplinary approach correctly
Sort questions about one event (a flood, a drought) into Geography, Economics, Political Science and History
Explain the spatial perspective and tools like maps, atlases and GIS
Define sustainable development and vasudhaiva kutumbakam
remember: Interdisciplinary approach: studying a problem using several disciplines together
Spatial perspective: where something happens and why that location matters
Vasudhaiva kutumbakam: 'the world is one family'
Sustainable development: meeting today's needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs
traps: 'Spatial' is about place, not 'special' and not time
Sustainable development does not mean no development, nor unlimited use
Don't study change over time without considering the place where it happened
